transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-09-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Nina Gomez (Redwood SE), Alex Wu (Redwood Solutions), Liam Chen (MeridianAI - Head of ML), Priya Kapoor (MeridianAI - Infra), Carlos Ruiz (MeridianAI - PM)

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we got about 55 minutes, want to cover capacity sizing, the reserved baseline, burst strategy and fallback policies for the POC, and then next steps
[00:12] Liam: thanks Samir, yeah, excited. quick context — we run a user-facing summarization service, peak at around 150-220 requests per second for short sessions, lots of 512-token outputs, sometimes spiky when marketing sends campaigns, and we need p95 latency pretty low.
[00:35] Priya: just to add, our infra is primarily in us-east-1, VPC, we need private networking for the POC if possible. also KMS for keys, and audit logs.
[00:50] Nina: got it, VPC + KMS noted. quick question on your traffic: are those sustained 200 rps or bursts?
[01:02] Liam: it's usually 80-120 sustained during day, and spikes to 200+ for 10-15 minutes a couple times a day. monthly average low.
[01:15] Alex: okay that helps. For POC we typically recommend a reserved baseline to cover sustained load and then a burst pool for short spikes — reduces cost while keeping latency SLOs.
[01:28] Carlos: what's the difference between reserved and burst in practice? like are burst nodes slower or cheaper?
[01:35] Nina: good question — burst is usually on-demand capacity, can be different instance types or shared pools, cost is higher per GPU but you only pay when used. performance should be similar, but warming KV caches and cold starts can add latency.
[01:52] Samir: and we can configure automatic fallback policies so if burst isn't avail we can route to smaller cheaper model variants or throttle non-critical requests.
[02:05] Priya: we need specifics — for example, if we reserve 2 A100-equivalent GPUs can that sustain 120 rps at 512 tokens?
[02:16] Nina: rough numbers: an A100-class GPU with optimized runtime and batching might do ~120-200 short responses depending on model. for 512 tokens with causal LM and batch sizes tuned, two GPUs should cover your sustained 100-120 rps with headroom. but we'll need to run a realistic benchmark with your payloads.
[02:40] Liam: ok so for POC we want reserved baseline for our day-to-day plus enough burst to hit 200 rps for 15 minutes. what's the recommended configuration for that?
[02:50] Alex: typical POC config: reserve capacity equivalent to 2 GPUs, and configure burst pool for up to 2-3 additional GPUs on demand. also enable KV caching for prefixes — that reduces tokens and improves tail latency for repeated prompts.
[03:07] Carlos: caching sounds promising, does Redwood support prefix caching across requests?
[03:12] Nina: yes, but caveat — cache hits depend on prompt variability. we can show cache hit rates in the benchmark. Also note KV cache handling differs per model and can be affected by quantization. sometimes transcripts show it as "K-V catch" in logs, so just be aware the naming is inconsistent in a few places.
[03:31] [00:03:35] Liam: haha noted. what's the expected warm-up time when scaling from 2 to 4 GPUs?
[03:40] Samir: there's two components: container start + runtime warm-up + KV cache. cold start can be 30-90s depending on image and node availability; we have warm pools and pre-warmed replicas option to reduce that to ~10-20s, but that increases baseline cost.
[03:58] Priya: pre-warmed replicas sound useful but we need pricing tradeoff. can you send options?
[04:05] Samir: yes we'll include pre-warm pricing. For POC we usually do small set of pre-warmed nodes for the burst pool to avoid long cold-starts.
[04:15] [00:04:20] Carlos: fallback — you mentioned model variants. do you mean degrade to a smaller model automatically? how does Redwood handle that?
[04:24] Nina: exactly. we support policy-based routing: if capacity constrained or latency thresholds breached, route to a compatible smaller model (e.g., 7B vs 13B) or to a local cached response. The policy can be tuned per route. Important to define accuracy tolerance in the success criteria.
[04:41] Liam: on accuracy — our product team wants <1% regression on key metrics (ROUGE/ROUGE-L for summarization) vs current baseline. If we route to smaller model during bursts that's acceptable only if regression is within that bound.
[04:55] Samir: that makes sense; will codify in SLOs. Also we can do A/B style test during POC to measure regression under burst conditions.
[05:05] Priya: timeline — we need a two-week POC. can Redwood support that? start benchmarks week of 9/22?
[05:13] Alex: yes two-week POC is common. timeline we propose: week 1: deploy reserved baseline, run initial benchmarks with sample traffic; week 2: run stress bursts, validate fallback policies, collect metrics and finalize SOW. target kickoff 2026-09-22 if you can deliver samples and access.
[05:31] [00:05:35] Liam: we can aim to share sample payloads by 9/22. security review also necessary — SOC 2 and SSO requirements.
[05:43] Samir: we'll send SOC2 pack and SAML/SSO docs. For private deployment options, do you need agent or Private (customer-managed) control plane for POC?
[05:55] Priya: for POC we prefer Private VPC endpoints and customer KMS. full Private-onprem not necessary yet.
[06:03] Nina: we can run POC in a VPC peering model, or with Private options. We'll include both in the SOW.
[06:10] Carlos: regarding metrics, we need p95 latency, p50, throughput, token cost per request, and cache hit ratio. Also per-route error rates and number of fallbacks triggered.
[06:22] Nina: we'll instrument and provide dashboards. Redwood Console gives token-level cost and per-model latency breakdowns.
[06:30] [00:06:35] Priya: what's the expected per-token cost difference between reserved and burst? ballpark numbers fine.
[06:37] Samir: reserved capacity amortizes GPU cost, so per-token is typically 30-50% cheaper than on-demand burst. exact depends on instance type and utilization. we'll put examples in the pricing sheet.
[06:50] Liam: ok. benchmark specifics — what scenarios should we run?
[06:55] Nina: recommended scenarios: 1) steady-state: sustained 100 rps for 30 minutes; 2) spike test: ramp 80->220 rps in <60s and hold 15 minutes; 3) cache-effectiveness: repeat prompts to measure prefix KV cache hit rate; 4) model-fallback: simulate burst when burst pool is exhausted to verify routing. We'll run each scenario a couple times.
[07:20] Carlos: will you need production traffic or can we do synthetic?
[07:24] Nina: sample payloads that reflect token distributions and prompt variability are best. If you can't share real data, we can synthesize but it's less accurate.
[07:33] [00:07:35] Priya: we'll provide anonymized samples and a traffic shape file.
[07:38] Samir: perfect — once we get that Nina will prepare the benchmark plan and scripts.
[07:44] Liam: one more — how do autoscaling thresholds work? do you autoscale on GPU utilization, queue depth, or latency?
[07:52] Nina: we support multiple signals. Most customers use a hybrid: scale-up on queue length or concurrency, with latency SLOs as safety. For example, if p95 > 100ms for 30s, trigger scale-up; also scale based on token-generation queue length.
[08:08] Priya: can we set hard caps to avoid runaway cost?
[08:12] Samir: yes, autoscale policies include max/min capacity and cost caps. We can also configure burst budget (e.g., 2 GPU-hours/day). We'll include those in the POC config.
[08:24] [00:08:30] Carlos: what's the recommended max for the POC? we want to test 4 GPU total.
[08:29] Alex: sounds good — baseline 2 reserved + burst up to 2 more = 4 max. set burst budget to limit costs during tests.
[08:37] Liam: ok. logging — we need audit logs for access and inference requests for compliance.
[08:43] Nina: audit logs and request-level tracing are available; retention configurable. We'll share retention options and costs.
[08:52] Priya: network egress — if we use dedicated capacity in customer VPC, egress is minimal, but if hosted there may be egress costs.
[08:59] Samir: we'll map out network topology in the SOW.
[09:05] [00:09:10] Carlos: anything else on fallback policies? I want to understand the user impact — i.e., when fallback routes to smaller model do we tag responses as degraded?
[09:15] Nina: yes you can add response headers or metadata indicating fallback and confidence score. We can also route only non-critical calls to degraded models to keep core UX consistent.
[09:27] Liam: for our use case we prefer degraded responses only for background summarizations, not for real-time UI updates.
[09:33] Samir: we'll build policy that preserves UI-critical routes.
[09:36] [00:09:40] Priya: okay next steps recap?
[09:39] Samir: recap: Samir sends SOW + POC pricing + SOC2 and SAML docs by 9/20. Priya sends traffic profile and sample payloads by 9/22. Nina prepares benchmark plan and test scripts by 9/23. We target benchmark kickoff week of 9/24 and finish POC in two weeks.
[09:56] Carlos: that works.
[09:59] Liam: quick question on SLA during POC, do you provide any uptime guarantees?
[10:03] Samir: POC doesn't include full SLA but we commit to uptime for the reserved nodes during the contract period; full SLA and support tiers are in Dedicated contract. We'll note expected availability for POC.
[10:16] [00:10:20] Priya: any sample dashboards we can see?
[10:22] Nina: yes we'll share Redwood Console screenshots and an example benchmark sheet.
[10:27] Samir: all right if no more questions we'll wrap. thanks everyone.
[10:31] Liam: thanks, great call.
[10:33] Carlos: thanks all.
[10:35] Samir: end call — follow-ups via email, will include pricing and security docs.

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcription had a few mislabels and some words like "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "K-V catch"; speaker labels corrected where obvious but some lines show timestamps with slight offsets.
